builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Agents Are Systems, Not Models: Rethinking Agentic Evaluation
summary: The paper replaces single success-rate evaluation of a fixed agent with evaluation of the agent as a configurable system, varying task information, reasoning, self-verification, time budget, and backbone model across repeated runs. Adoption costs multiple evaluation runs per configuration (the study used over 18,000 trajectories) plus engineering effort to expose configuration knobs and implement dedicated verification tools rather than relying on prompt instructions. Failures include mistaking run-to-run stochasticity for real improvement when run counts are low, and wasted compute from extending time budgets when the agent lacks sufficient task information or a capable model to use the extra time.
rationale: The findings translate directly into low-cost production practice for a constrained team: invest in task information and tool-based verification, evaluate across repeated runs, and treat configuration as a first-class variable rather than scaling model size or time budget blindly.

claims.statement: The paper replaces single success-rate evaluation of a fixed agent with evaluation of the agent as a configurable system, varying task information, reasoning, self-verification, time budget, and backbone model across repeated runs. Adoption costs multiple evaluation runs per configuration (the study used over 18,000 trajectories) plus engineering effort to expose configuration knobs and implement dedicated verification tools rather than relying on prompt instructions. Failures include mistaking run-to-run stochasticity for real improvement when run counts are low, and wasted compute from extending time budgets when the agent lacks sufficient task information or a capable model to use the extra time.

Across configurations, task information had the largest effect on performance, exceeding time budget and model size, while also reducing cost and improving calibration; approximately 54% of outcome variance came from repeating the same configuration rather than changing it.
